title: Mara defeated
hookLine: the army scatters; a voice from the sky tells Mara to give up (Buddhacarita 13)

cards: The army doesn't stop to talk. Mara has already tried talking: a speech about duty, a flower arrow, and the man under the tree didn't stir. So now everything the army can lift, it throws.
Rocks, trees, spears, fire. The air around the tree fills with howling and smoke. In the middle of it, one man sits with his legs crossed and his eyes steady.
He doesn't answer. He doesn't flinch. And then a voice speaks from somewhere above the noise, from someone nobody can see.

teach.b: First, the attack. The poem gives the army full force. Some hurl boulders.
Some swing whole trees. Some throw weapons, some breathe fire, some try to terrify him with shrieks and faces. Second, what happens to it.
Nothing lands. In paraphrase, what's thrown at him stops in the air, or falls short, or turns harmless. The fire doesn't burn him.
The noise doesn't move him. Third, the voice. A being in the sky, unseen, speaks to Mara: give up this useless effort.
You can no more shake this man than the wind can shake the great mountain. Fire might lose its heat, water its wetness, the earth its firmness, before he gives up his resolve.
He has made his vow, and the time has come for it to be fulfilled. Fourth, the scattering.
Mara looks at the man under the tree, still unmoved, and the poem says he goes away disheartened, his effort spent, and his army scatters in every direction. The sky clears. Flowers fall from it.
Look at how the victory is won. The prince never lifts a hand, never argues back, never calls for help. The poem doesn't even give him a line.
His whole answer is to keep sitting, and the army, which could break anything that resisted, has nothing to push against.
What scatters it isn't a stronger army. It's stillness that won't be moved.

how: Buddhist art shows the Buddha seated at the moment of victory over Mara, and in some traditions the story is retold at festivals of the awakening.

games.q: the night Mara lost: tap the pairs.
p: stop in the air or turn harmless

s: in the poem, the prince fights back against Mara's army
he never lifts a hand; he keeps sitting, and the army fails.
a voice from the sky compares him to a mountain the wind can't shake
it tells Mara to give up his useless effort.
Mara is killed under the tree
he goes away disheartened, and his army scatters.

games.q: you're Mara. your flower arrow failed, and now your whole army has failed too. a voice from the sky tells you to give up. what do you do?
o: sit down beside him and learn.
games.why: Mara looks once more at the unmoved man and goes away disheartened. his army scatters, the sky clears, and flowers fall.

practice: Bring back the fear you named yesterday, or another that's here today, and let it come close without pushing it away or following it.

Keep sitting, the way the prince keeps sitting while the army howls, and feel the breath come in and go out underneath it. If the fear thins, let it thin; if it stays, that's all right, and keep breathing.

wordCard.voice: Mara defeated. The army throws everything at the seated prince and nothing lands; a voice from the sky tells Mara to give up, and his army scatters. Today's word.

orig.note: Sanskrit: unmoving, steady; also a word for a mountain.

carryVoice: Your line: the army scatters. Tomorrow the night goes on, and the poem turns from what he refused to what he sees. That's day seven hundred sixteen.
